title: Legal Skills and Methodology

sources.title: University of Cambridge undergraduate course page: Law BA (Hons)
sources.used_for: description of the compulsory online pre-arrival 'Legal Skills and Methodology' self-study course; Part IA papers, teaching pattern and assessment

about: Legal Skills and Methodology is a compulsory online, self-study pre-arrival course that incoming Cambridge law students complete before starting Part IA; the University says it will help develop legal understanding and associated skills, and that details are sent before arrival. The University does not publish its detailed content or say whether it is assessed, and it is not among the Part IA papers listed on the course page. This guide therefore explains what is confirmed about the course and then gives general preparation in legal method for England and Wales (reading cases, precedent, statutory interpretation, answering questions); that general material is not the official course content.
topics: Reading cases and the doctrine of precedent
Getting ready for Part IA supervisions and exams

notes.body:
Before starting Part IA of the Cambridge Law Tripos, every incoming law student must complete an online pre-arrival course. The University describes it as a self-study programme focused on "Legal Skills and Methodology", designed to develop your legal understanding and the skills that go with it. Details are sent to you before you arrive in Cambridge.

What we can and cannot confirm
- Confirmed: it is online, self-study, compulsory for incoming students, completed before Part IA begins, and focused on legal skills and method.
- Not stated on the University's course page: its detailed content, how long it takes, or whether it is formally assessed. It is not listed as one of the Part IA examined papers (in recent years these have been Civil Law in Context, Constitutional Law, Criminal Law and Law of Tort).
- So this pack does not set out a syllabus for the programme. Follow the materials you are sent. The notes that follow cover general legal method that every Part IA paper relies on, so you can use them alongside the official course.

Why it matters
Part IA teaching moves quickly. The University's course page says you will usually have 10 to 12 hours of lectures, and one supervision for each paper every two weeks; supervisions normally involve preparing work in advance. Supervisors expect you to be able to:
- find and read a law report and identify what the court decided and why;
- find the relevant section of a statute and read it closely;
- use authority accurately in written answers;
- tackle problem questions and essays in a structured way.
Getting these habits right before term starts makes the first weeks of supervisions much easier.

Exam tips: whatever form the pre-arrival course takes, these skills are tested throughout the Part IA papers through accurate use of cases and statutes and well-structured answers.

General preparation (not official course content). The law of England and Wales is built partly on decided cases. You need to read judgments efficiently and know which ones bind which courts.

Anatomy of a law report
- Case name (e.g. R v Jogee), citation, court and judges.
- Headnote: a summary written by the reporter, not part of the judgment. Useful for orientation, but never cite it as the court's reasoning.
- Facts, procedural history, arguments, and the judgments themselves. In appellate courts there may be several judgments, including dissents.

Citations
- Neutral citations identify the court and judgment number, e.g. [2016] UKSC 8 (Supreme Court), [2020] EWCA Crim 575 (Court of Appeal, Criminal Division), [2002] EWHC 195 (Admin) (High Court, Administrative Court).
- Law report citations identify the series, e.g. [1999] 1 AC 82 (Appeal Cases) or [1934] 1 KB 590. Square brackets mean the year is essential to find the volume; round brackets mean it is not.

Ratio and obiter
- The ratio decidendi is the legal principle necessary for the decision on the material facts. It is binding on lower courts (and usually on the same court).
- Obiter dicta are other statements of law, such as comments on hypothetical facts or points not needed for the decision. They can be highly persuasive (e.g. the dicta on sovereignty in Jackson [2005]) but do not bind.
- Finding the ratio of a case with several judgments means looking for the reasoning shared by the majority.

The hierarchy and precedent (England and Wales)
- The Supreme Court binds all lower courts. It can depart from its own (and House of Lords) decisions under the 1966 Practice Statement, [1966] 1 WLR 1234, but does so rarely; Austin v Southwark LBC [2010] UKSC 28 confirmed the Supreme Court inherited this power.
- The Court of Appeal (Civil Division) is generally bound by its own decisions, subject to the exceptions in Young v Bristol Aeroplane Co [1944] KB 718 (conflicting decisions, decisions inconsistent with a higher court, and decisions made per incuriam).
- The High Court binds lower courts.
- Privy Council decisions are persuasive only. In Willers v Joyce (No 2) [2016] UKSC 44 the Supreme Court said lower courts may follow a Privy Council decision in preference to a binding one if the Privy Council expressly says it is stating English law.

Techniques
- Distinguishing: showing the material facts differ, so the earlier ratio does not apply.
- Overruling: a higher court declares an earlier decision wrong in law (e.g. R v G [2003] overruling Caldwell).

Exam tips: when you cite a case, state the proposition it supports in one line. Do not retell the facts unless they matter to your argument.

General preparation (not official course content), for England and Wales. Much of the law you study in Part IA is statutory (e.g. the Theft Act 1968, the Human Rights Act 1998, the Coroners and Justice Act 2009). Reading a statute closely is a core skill.

Finding your way round an Act
- Short title and year (e.g. Theft Act 1968), and a long title stating its general purpose.
- Sections, subsections and paragraphs: cite them precisely, e.g. "Theft Act 1968, s 1(1)" or "s 76(5A)".
- Schedules contain detail, such as the list of reserved matters in Schedule 5 to the Scotland Act 1998.
- Commencement: an Act may be in force only partly, or from dates set by regulations. Check the version in force on legislation.gov.uk and note amendments.
- Secondary (delegated) legislation, such as statutory instruments, is made by ministers under powers in an Act and is cited by year and number.

Approaches to interpretation
Courts aim to identify the meaning Parliament intended, read in context.
- Literal rule: words are given their ordinary meaning even if the result seems odd (Whiteley v Chappell (1868)).
- Golden rule: the literal meaning may be modified to avoid absurdity (Adler v George [1964] 2 QB 7).
- Mischief rule: identify the mischief the Act was meant to remedy (Heydon's Case (1584)); e.g. Smith v Hughes [1960] 1 WLR 830, where soliciting from a window counted as soliciting "in a street".
- The modern purposive and contextual approach: words are read in the context of the Act as a whole and its purpose. The Supreme Court summarised this in R (O) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2022] UKSC 3, treating external aids as secondary to the words themselves.
- Hansard may be consulted where the legislation is ambiguous or obscure (or its literal meaning leads to absurdity), the statement relied on was made by a minister or other promoter of the Bill, and the statement is clear (Pepper v Hart [1993] AC 593).

Presumptions and statutory directions
- The presumption that mens rea is required for criminal offences (Sweet v Parsley [1970] AC 132).
- The principle of legality: general words do not override fundamental rights (R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex p Simms [2000] 2 AC 115).
- The presumption against retrospective effect.
- Human Rights Act 1998, s 3: legislation must be read compatibly with Convention rights so far as possible.
- The Interpretation Act 1978 supplies standard definitions (e.g. words in the singular include the plural).

Exam tips: quote or closely paraphrase the exact statutory words that matter, then show how the courts have interpreted them.

General preparation (not official course content). Cambridge teaches law through lectures, seminars and small-group supervisions, and Part IA is assessed mostly through examinations at the end of the year; you will not usually be able to resit. Good method from the start pays off.

Reading and notes
- Read primary sources (cases and statutes) as well as textbooks. For leading cases, read at least the key passages of the main judgment.
- Keep notes organised by topic. For each case record: citation, court, one-line facts, the ratio, and any important dissent or obiter.
- After each topic, write a one-page summary of the rules and the main debates.

Answering problem questions
A common structure (often called IRAC) works well:
- Issue: identify each legal issue raised by the facts, party by party.
- Rule: state the legal rule precisely, with authority (statute section or case).
- Application: apply the rule to the facts, including facts that cut both ways.
- Conclusion: reach a reasoned answer, saying how likely it is when the law is uncertain.
Deal with the points the facts actually raise; avoid writing everything you know about the topic.

Writing essays
- Answer the question set. Identify the claim in the title and take a position.
- Plan an argument: each paragraph should advance it and be supported by authority (cases, statutes, academic views).
- Engage with counter-arguments and conclude by returning to the question.

Citing authority
- Use a consistent citation style. OSCOLA (the Oxford University Standard for Citation of Legal Authorities) is widely used in UK law schools; check what your Faculty or supervisor asks for.
- Cite statutes by short title, year and section; cases with their citation the first time.

Supervisions
- Submit written work on time and read the feedback carefully.
- Come with questions; supervisions are for testing your understanding, not for repeating lectures.

Exam tips: practise timed answers from past papers in the months before the exams, and plan before you write. A clear structure and accurate use of authority usually matter more than covering every case.

questions.q: Which part of a judgment binds lower courts?
questions.why: Only the ratio binds. The headnote is written by the reporter, not the court; obiter dicta and dissents can be persuasive but are not binding.

questions.q: Under Young v Bristol Aeroplane Co, in which situation may the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) depart from its own previous decision?
options: Whenever it thinks the earlier decision was wrong
Where the earlier decision was made per incuriam
Where the earlier decision was by a High Court judge
Where the earlier decision was reported more than 50 years ago
questions.why: The three exceptions are conflicting CA decisions, inconsistency with a higher court decision, and per incuriam decisions. The CA does not have a general power to depart (unlike the Supreme Court under the 1966 Practice Statement); High Court decisions never bind it; age is irrelevant.

questions.q: In Pepper v Hart [1993], when did the House of Lords allow courts to refer to Hansard?
options: Where the legislation is ambiguous or obscure, the statement is by a minister or promoter, and it is clear
questions.why: Pepper v Hart set these three conditions. Before it, Hansard was generally excluded; it is not freely available as an aid, and the rule is not limited to criminal statutes.

questions.q: Which approach to statutory interpretation asks what problem the Act was passed to remedy?
questions.why: The mischief rule comes from Heydon's Case (1584). The literal rule gives words their plain meaning; the golden rule avoids absurdity; ejusdem generis reads general words in light of a list of specific ones.

questions.q: Explain how you would structure an answer to a problem question in a Part IA law exam.
markScheme: Identify each issue raised by the facts, party by party
State the relevant rule precisely with authority (case or statute section)
Apply the rule to the facts, including facts pointing both ways
Reach a reasoned conclusion, indicating uncertainty where the law is unclear
questions.modelAnswer: Start by identifying each legal issue the facts raise, taking each party or incident in turn. For each issue, state the governing rule precisely and support it with authority, such as a statutory section or a leading case. Then apply the rule to the facts, using the specific details given and considering arguments on both sides. Finish each issue with a reasoned conclusion, saying how likely an outcome is where the law is uncertain, and end with a brief overall conclusion. Keep to the issues the facts actually raise.
